Tintinalli Chapter 193

Digitalis Glycosides

Digoxin toxicity is a potassium, rhythm, renal-function, and antidote-timing chapter.

MCQ 28Source images 4Crop QA PASS

Overview

Digitalis glycosides include pharmaceutical digoxin and plant or animal cardiac glycosides such as foxglove, oleander, lily of the valley, and toad toxins. Toxicity matters because it can present as vague GI/CNS complaints or sudden unstable dysrhythmia.

The ED frame is simple but unforgiving: identify acute vs chronic exposure, check rhythm and potassium, do not trust early levels blindly, and give digoxin-specific antibody fragments when severe features appear.

Rosen source check

ED tox stabilization

Rosen supports the same bedside priorities: stabilize ABCs, continuous ECG monitoring, treat life-threatening bradyarrhythmias/ventricular dysrhythmias, correct electrolytes, and use antidote early when severe toxicity is present.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli supplies the digitalis-specific presentation and Fab calculation tables; Rosen reinforces unstable-patient management and poison center/toxicology escalation.

Pathophysiology and Risk

Digoxin inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase. Intracellular sodium rises, sodium-calcium exchange is impaired, intracellular calcium rises, and inotropy increases. Toxicity also increases vagal tone and automaticity, producing bradydysrhythmias, AV block, ventricular ectopy, and nearly any rhythm except rapidly conducted atrial arrhythmias.

Chronic toxicity is promoted by renal dysfunction, older age, low lean body mass, diuretics, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and interacting drugs such as amiodarone, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, indomethacin, procainamide, and erythromycin.

Clinical Features

Acute toxicity often starts with GI symptoms and may show hyperkalemia; chronic toxicity often appears in older cardiac patients with weakness, fatigue, confusion, delirium, renal insufficiency, and rhythm disturbance. The digoxin level may be therapeutic in chronic toxicity and falsely high early after acute ingestion.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is composite: history, medications, renal function, ECG, potassium, magnesium, and properly timed digoxin levels. A level obtained before 6 hours after acute ingestion reflects distribution and should not delay treatment in an unstable patient.

Do now

ECG, potassium, magnesium, creatinine, serial digoxin level when relevant, medication review, and plant/toad exposure history.

Do not do

Do not diagnose toxicity from scooped ST segments alone. Do not wait for a confirmatory level when the patient has hyperkalemia plus life-threatening dysrhythmia.

Rosen source check

Differential diagnosis

Rosen ED differential framing keeps look-alikes active: beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, clonidine, class I antiarrhythmics, conduction disease, and other causes of hyperkalemic bradycardia can mimic digitalis toxicity.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli gives digoxin-specific diagnostic caveats; Rosen strengthens the broad ED differential so a conduction-poisoning patient is not mislabeled too early.

Treatment

Treatment starts with supportive care, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, correction of hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia in chronic toxicity, and anticipation of severe complications. Activated charcoal can be considered for early acute ingestion in an awake, cooperative, protected-airway patient.

For life-threatening bradyarrhythmias, temporize with atropine and/or transcutaneous pacing while obtaining Fab. For ventricular irritability, magnesium may help. Calcium for recognized digoxin-induced hyperkalemia remains controversial and should be avoided when Fab is available.

Digoxin-Specific Antibody Fragments

Digoxin-Fab is the treatment of choice for acute poisoning with potassium >5.0 mEq/L or acute/chronic toxicity with life-threatening dysrhythmia. It removes free digoxin from tissue and can rapidly reverse rhythm toxicity.

Watch for hypokalemia after Fab, worsening heart failure, increased ventricular response in atrial fibrillation, and misleading total digoxin levels after Fab. In renal failure, delayed recurrent toxicity can occur as Fab-digoxin complex persists.

Rosen source check

Antidote timing

Rosen antidote logic aligns with Tintinalli: severe clinical toxicity is enough to treat. A deteriorating patient should receive Fab based on clinical severity, potassium, and rhythm, not wait for a perfect dose calculation.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli gives calculation formulas; Rosen emphasizes antidote-first decision-making in unstable poisonings.

Drug Dose Reference

This is a quick recap after the treatment narrative and Fab calculation table above. In real severe cases, involve poison center/toxicology early.

InterventionTypical adult useKey warning
Activated charcoal1 g/kg PO/NG early acute ingestion if awake/protected airwayAvoid if obtunded/unprotected airway.
Atropine0.5-1 mg IV as temporizing bradyarrhythmia treatmentBridge while Fab/pacing arranged.
Digoxin-FabDose by ingested amount or serum concentration; empiric vials when unstable/unknownMonitor potassium and rhythm closely.
MagnesiumConsider for ventricular irritabilityClinical/toxicology guided.
